text: A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
reflection: Some friendships last only as long as things are easy. When life gets complicated, those friends quietly disappear. Proverbs describes something better: "A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity." At all times. In seasons of success and seasons of loss. When you are fun to be around and when you are struggling. A true friend does not keep a schedule of availability based on convenience. And the second half of the verse adds a striking thought. A brother is born for adversity. Hard times reveal what relationships are made of. They are the very moments real friendship was designed for. Think of the people who stayed with you through a difficult season. Give thanks to God for them, and maybe tell them how much it meant. Then ask yourself whether there is someone going through adversity right now who needs a friend who loves at all times. You may be the answer to their prayer.
question: Who stood by you in a hard season, and who might need you to stand by them now?
prayer: Lord, thank You for the friends who loved me at all times, even in adversity. Make me that kind of friend to someone who is struggling today. Amen.

text: A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
reflection: Loneliness is one of the quiet struggles of our time. Many people long for close friends but are unsure how to find them. Proverbs offers practical wisdom: "A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly." Friendship usually begins with someone taking the first step. A greeting, an invitation, a question, a word of encouragement. Waiting for others to reach out can leave us waiting a long time. Being friendly is not about having a big personality. It is about showing genuine interest in others. Then the verse lifts our eyes higher: "there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother." Some human friendships reach that level of closeness, and they are treasures. But ultimately this points us to the faithfulness of God, who never leaves us. Even when human friends are few, we are not friendless. Today, take a small step of friendliness toward someone. And rest in the One who sticks closer than any brother.
question: What step of friendliness could you take toward someone today?
prayer: Lord, help me show myself friendly, and give me courage to reach out first. Thank You that You are the Friend who sticks closer than a brother. Amen.

text: Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
reflection: King Solomon had wealth, power, and wisdom, and he spent much of Ecclesiastes asking what truly matters in life. One of his conclusions was simple: "Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour." Work done together often accomplishes more than work done alone. Burdens shared are lighter. Joys shared are fuller. Solomon had seen people who worked endlessly by themselves, piling up riches with no one to share them, and he called that vanity. Life was not designed to be lived in isolation. God made us for relationship, with Him and with each other. Independence is often praised, but there is wisdom in partnership. Perhaps there is a task you have been trying to carry alone. Could you invite someone to help? Or perhaps someone near you is working hard without support. Could you come alongside them? Two really are better than one. Look for ways to share the work and the reward today.
question: What task could you share today, or whom could you come alongside?
prayer: Lord, You made us for partnership, not isolation. Show me someone I can work with and walk beside today, and let us both be stronger for it. Amen.

text: For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.
reflection: Solomon continued with a vivid picture: "For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up." Everyone falls sometimes. We stumble into sin, slip into discouragement, or get knocked down by circumstances beyond our control. The question is not whether we will fall, but whether anyone will be there to help us up. Solomon describes the person who falls alone as one to be pitied. There is no hand reaching down, no voice of encouragement, no one to say, you can get up again. This is why friendship matters so much. It is not only for good times. It is a safety net for hard ones. Today, think of whether you have people who would help you up, and whether you are that person for someone else. If someone you know has fallen, do not stand back. Reach out your hand.
question: Who around you has fallen or is struggling, and how could you help lift them up?
prayer: Lord, open my eyes to anyone who has fallen and has no one to help them rise. Make me the friend who reaches out a hand today. Amen.

text: And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God…
reflection: Naomi had lost her husband and both her sons in a foreign land. She decided to return home to Bethlehem and urged her widowed daughters-in-law to go back to their own families. One of them, Orpah, tearfully agreed. But Ruth refused: "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Ruth had every reason to leave. Naomi had nothing to offer her: no money, no husband, no security. Yet Ruth chose loyalty. She bound her life to Naomi's and to Naomi's God. That decision changed history. Ruth later married Boaz and became the great-grandmother of King David. Loyal love is rare and beautiful. It stays when leaving would be easier. It chooses commitment over comfort. Is there someone in your life who needs that kind of loyalty from you? Stand by them today. Faithful love often matters more than we will ever know.
question: Who needs your loyal love right now, even when leaving would be easier?
prayer: Lord, give me the loyal love of Ruth, love that stays when it would be easier to go. Help me be faithful to the people You have placed in my life. Amen.

text: And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
reflection: After David defeated Goliath, he stood before King Saul, and Saul's son Jonathan was watching. Something happened in that moment: "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." It was an unlikely friendship. Jonathan was the prince, the heir to the throne. David was a shepherd boy who would one day take that throne. Jonathan could have seen David as a rival. Instead, he saw a brother. He gave David his robe, his sword, and his bow. Later, he risked his own life to protect David from his father's anger. Knit is a beautiful word. It describes threads woven together so closely they become one fabric. True friendship knits lives together. It is selfless and loyal, and it seeks the good of the other even at personal cost. Thank God today for friends whose lives are woven with yours. And ask Him to make you a Jonathan to someone.
question: Is there someone you could choose to support today instead of seeing them as a rival?
prayer: Lord, thank You for friends whose hearts are knit with mine. Free me from rivalry and envy, and teach me to love others as Jonathan loved David. Amen.

text: Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
reflection: A dull knife can be sharpened by rubbing it against another piece of iron. The process involves friction and sparks, but the result is a blade that works as it should. Proverbs applies that picture to relationships: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend." Good friends make each other better. They challenge our thinking, encourage our growth, and sometimes point out where we have grown dull. That process is not always comfortable. There may be friction. But it is a gift. A friend who only ever agrees with you may be pleasant, but they will not help you grow. Look for friends who love God and love you enough to sharpen you. And be that kind of friend for others. Ask good questions. Share what God is teaching you. Encourage someone to take the next step of faith. Sharpening is a two-way exchange. Both pieces of iron come away better than before.
question: Who helps sharpen you, and how could you be a sharpening friend to someone else?
prayer: Lord, as iron sharpens iron, let my friendships make us both better. Give me friends who help me grow, and make me that kind of friend in return. Amen.

text: Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
reflection: Not everything that feels kind is kind, and not everything that hurts is harmful. Proverbs puts it sharply: "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful." A true friend will sometimes tell you what you do not want to hear. They will point out a blind spot, warn you about a bad decision, or gently confront a sin. Those words can sting. But they come from love. A flatterer, on the other hand, may say only pleasant things while caring nothing for your good. Flattery feels nice but leaves you unchanged. Honest love may hurt for a moment, but it heals. This verse challenges us in two directions. First, will we receive hard truth from those who love us without getting defensive? Second, will we love others enough to speak honestly when needed, with gentleness and care? Today, thank God for friends who are honest with you. Their wounds are faithful.
question: Is there honest counsel you need to receive with grace, or a truth you need to speak in love?
prayer: Lord, faithful are the wounds of a friend. Give me humility to receive honest words, and wisdom to speak hard truths with love and care. Amen.

text: Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you.
reflection: On the night before His crucifixion, Jesus spoke tenderly to His disciples. They had followed Him for three years as students and servants. Now He gave them a new title: "Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends." A servant does what he is told without knowing the master's plans. A friend is let in on the purpose. Jesus had shared with them everything the Father had shown Him. He had opened His heart. This is astonishing. The Lord of all creation calls ordinary people His friends. He does not merely give orders; He shares His heart. That same friendship is offered to every believer. You are not just a servant trying to earn approval. You are a friend of Jesus, invited to know Him and walk with Him. Today, talk to Him as a friend. Share your heart, listen to His, and enjoy His company.
question: What would you say to Jesus today if you spoke to Him as a trusted friend?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You call me Your friend and share the Father's words with me. Thank You for that friendship. Let me talk with You today with an open heart. Amen.

text: Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another…
reflection: Paul's letter to the Romans contains a whole chapter on how believers should treat one another. In the middle of it is this instruction: "Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another." Kindly affectioned describes the warm care of family members. It is not cold politeness but genuine tenderness. And in honour preferring one another means trying to outdo each other in showing respect. Imagine a community where people compete not to get ahead, but to lift each other up. Where everyone is looking for ways to celebrate others rather than themselves. That is the picture Paul paints. It runs against our natural instinct to seek our own recognition. But it is exactly how Christ treated us. He humbled Himself and put our good above His own. Today, look for a way to honour someone else. Give credit, offer praise, step back so another can shine. Let warm affection guide the way you treat everyone you meet.
question: Whom could you honour today ahead of yourself?
prayer: Lord, give me kindly affection for the people around me. Free me from seeking recognition, and help me find joy in honouring others today. Amen.

text: Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
reflection: This verse is short but challenging: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." At first it sounds simple. Of course we should share in others' joys and sorrows. But in practice, both halves can be hard. Rejoicing with others can be difficult when their good news highlights our own disappointments. A friend gets the job, the engagement, the healing, the open door we have been praying for. Celebrating sincerely takes humility. Weeping with others can be hard too. It is uncomfortable to sit with someone's pain. We want to fix it, explain it, or move past it quickly. But often what grieving people need most is presence. Someone who will simply weep with them. Love enters into another person's experience. It does not stand at a distance. Today, look around you. Is someone celebrating? Rejoice with them wholeheartedly. Is someone hurting? Sit with them. Let your heart move with theirs.
question: Whose joy or sorrow could you share with your whole heart today?
prayer: Lord, teach me to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep. Give me a humble heart that enters fully into the lives of others. Amen.

text: Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
reflection: Everyone carries burdens. Some are visible: illness, financial strain, a demanding job. Others are hidden: anxiety, grief, temptation, loneliness. Paul gives a clear instruction to the church: "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." Bearing a burden means getting underneath it with someone. It means helping them carry what is too heavy for them alone. That might look like a meal, a phone call, a prayer, an hour of practical help, or a listening ear. And Paul says that when we do this, we fulfil the law of Christ. Jesus summed up the law as loving God and loving our neighbour. Carrying someone's load is love in action. It is also exactly what Jesus did for us. He bore our heaviest burden, our sin, on Himself. Today, ask God to show you someone whose load you can help carry. Then step in. Your shoulder might be the relief they have been praying for.
question: Whose burden could you help carry today, even in a small way?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You carried my load when I could not. Show me someone whose burden I can help bear today, and let my help be love in action. Amen.

text: Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up…
reflection: Paul's famous description of love begins with two qualities: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind." The word charity in the King James Version means self-giving love. Suffering long means being patient, especially with people. It means putting up with weaknesses, delays, and irritations without giving up on someone. Kindness is the active side of that patience. It is not merely tolerating others but doing them good. Paul then lists what love does not do. It does not envy. It does not boast. It is not puffed up with pride. These are the habits that quietly poison relationships. Envy resents others' blessings. Boasting draws attention to ourselves. Pride looks down on others. Love lets all of that go. It is patient, kind, content, and humble. No one does this perfectly. But God's love for us is exactly like this, and His Spirit can grow it in us. Today, choose patience with someone who tests you. Then go further and be kind.
question: Who needs your patience and active kindness today?
prayer: Lord, Your love is patient and kind. Where I am quick to envy, boast, or grow impatient, change my heart, and let me show kindness to someone today. Amen.

text: A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
reflection: Words have power. They can calm a storm or start one. Proverbs puts it plainly: "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger." We have all experienced both. A tense conversation suddenly cools because someone responds gently. Or a minor disagreement explodes because someone answers harshly. The difference is often a single sentence. A soft answer does not mean a weak answer. It is not agreeing with everything or avoiding the truth. It means speaking with gentleness, calm, and respect, even when the other person is upset. It takes strength to answer softly when we are criticized or misunderstood. Our instinct is to defend ourselves or hit back. But gentle words have a remarkable ability to defuse anger. Today, pay attention to your tone, especially with the people closest to you. When tension rises, take a breath and choose a soft answer. You may be surprised at how quickly the heat goes out of the room.
question: Where is tension likely to rise today, and how could you prepare a soft answer?
prayer: Lord, a soft answer turns away wrath. When tension rises today, give me the strength to answer gently, and guard my tongue from harsh words. Amen.

text: Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil…
reflection: Paul's description of love continues with qualities that touch everyday life: love "Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil." Love is not rude. It does not demand its own way. It is not touchy or quick to take offence. And it thinks no evil, which means it does not keep a record of wrongs or assume the worst. Think about how much conflict comes from these very things. We act rudely when we are tired. We insist on our way. We are easily irritated. We keep score of every offence and bring up old hurts. Love chooses a different path. It lets small things go. It gives the benefit of the doubt. It assumes good motives rather than bad. None of us love like this by nature, but it is how God loves us. He does not keep a ledger of our failures. Today, release a grudge. Choose to think the best of someone.
question: Is there a grudge you are keeping score on that you could let go of today?
prayer: Lord, love keeps no record of wrongs. Help me let go of the grudges I have been holding, and teach me to think the best of others. Amen.

text: With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love…
reflection: Living closely with other people reveals our rough edges. Families, roommates, coworkers, and church members all discover each other's quirks and flaws. Paul knew this, so he urged believers to live together "With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love." Forbearing means putting up with, bearing patiently. It assumes that people will sometimes be difficult. They will annoy us, disappoint us, and see things differently. Love does not demand that others become perfect before we accept them. It makes room for their weaknesses. Paul pairs this with lowliness and meekness, because forbearing is easier when we remember our own flaws. Others are putting up with us too. Longsuffering adds endurance to the mix. This is not a one-time effort but a daily choice. Today, think of someone who tests your patience. Ask God for grace to bear with them in love, remembering how patiently He bears with you.
question: Who tests your patience, and how could you bear with them in love today?
prayer: Lord, clothe me with humility, gentleness, and patience. Help me bear with others in love, remembering how patiently You bear with me. Amen.

text: And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.
reflection: In Colossians 3, Paul lists the qualities believers should put on like clothing: mercy, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, and forgiveness. Then he adds one final garment: "And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness." Love is like a belt that holds all the other garments in place. Without it, the other virtues can become cold and mechanical. Kindness without love can be a performance. Patience without love can be grudging endurance. But love ties everything together into a complete, beautiful whole. The word bond also suggests unity. Love is what binds people together. In families, friendships, and communities, love is the glue that holds us close when differences threaten to pull us apart. Put on love today the way you put on your clothes in the morning. Make it a deliberate choice. Let it hold together every other good thing God is growing in you.
question: Where has your kindness or patience grown cold, and how could you put on love today?
prayer: Lord, above all things I put on love, the bond that holds everything together. Warm my heart, and let love shape every kindness I show today. Amen.

text: Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
reflection: Gardeners know that a young tree can be gently shaped. With careful support, it grows straight and strong. An old tree is much harder to change. Proverbs applies that wisdom to raising children: "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it." Training is more than telling. It involves example, patience, and repetition. Children learn far more from what they see than from what they hear. They watch how we speak, how we handle frustration, how we treat others, and whether we pray. This verse encourages parents, grandparents, teachers, and anyone who influences a young life. The investment matters. The habits and values planted early often last a lifetime. And even when a child wanders for a time, the seeds sown in love are not wasted. If you have young people in your life, pray for them today. Then show them, by your own example, the way they should go.
question: Which young person in your life could you pray for and set an example for today?
prayer: Lord, I lift up the young people in my life. Help me show them Your way more by my example than by my words, and keep them on Your path. Amen.

text: Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
reflection: The Ten Commandments begin with our relationship to God. Then, as they turn to our relationships with each other, the very first one addresses the family: "Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee." Paul later noted that this is the first commandment with a promise attached. To honour means to give weight, to treat as valuable. It includes respect, gratitude, and care. For children, it means obedience. For adults, it may mean listening, visiting, supporting aging parents, and speaking of them with respect. This commandment does not require pretending parents are perfect. Some parents have deeply hurt their children, and honour may look different in those situations. But wherever possible, God calls us to treat our parents with dignity. If your parents are living, consider how you can honour them this week. If they have passed, give thanks for the good they gave you.
question: How could you honour your parents today, or give thanks to God for them?
prayer: Lord, thank You for my father and mother. Help me honour them with respect and gratitude, even where they were imperfect, and bless them by Your grace. Amen.

text: And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
reflection: Right after telling children to obey their parents, Paul turns to those with authority in the home: "And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord." In Paul's day, fathers had almost total power over their children. Paul limits that power with love. Parents are not to exasperate their children with harshness, unfair demands, constant criticism, or inconsistency. Instead, they are to nurture them. Nurture means caring for and training, like tending a growing plant. Admonition means gentle instruction and correction. Both are to be of the Lord, shaped by His character and His Word. This verse speaks to anyone who has authority over others, whether at home, at work, or in a community. Authority is given to build people up, not to crush them. Today, if you lead others in any way, ask whether your words and actions nurture or provoke. Lead the way God leads you: firmly, patiently, and with love.
question: Does your leadership build up those in your care, or wear them down?
prayer: Lord, whatever authority You have given me, help me use it to build others up and not crush them. Teach me to nurture and instruct with Your patience. Amen.

text: Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward.
reflection: In the ancient world, children were sometimes seen mainly as workers or as a way to carry on the family name. Psalm 127 lifts our view: "Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward." A heritage is a gift passed down, an inheritance. Children are not possessions we create but gifts God entrusts to us. They belong first to Him. This changes how we see them. Every child, whether our own or someone else's, has worth because God gave them. They are not interruptions or burdens but blessings to be treasured and raised with care. This verse also speaks to those who have longed for children, and to those who have lost them. God sees that longing and grief. And many people who are not parents still pour themselves into the lives of children as teachers, mentors, aunts, uncles, and friends. Today, thank God for the children in your life. Treat them as the gifts they are.
question: How could you treat the children in your life as a treasure from God today?
prayer: Lord, children are a heritage from You. Thank You for the children in my life. Help me treat them as treasures entrusted to me, with patience and love. Amen.

text: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
reflection: Psalm 133 was a song sung by travellers on their way up to Jerusalem. People from many towns and tribes walked the roads together. As they gathered, they sang, "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" Good and pleasant. Some things are good but not pleasant, like medicine. Some are pleasant but not good, like too much dessert. Unity is both. It is right before God, and it is a joy to experience. Unity does not mean everyone is the same. The tribes of Israel had different histories, regions, and personalities. Unity means being joined by something greater than our differences. For believers, that is our shared relationship with God. Disunity is painful. Families fractured by feuds, friendships ended by misunderstandings, communities divided by pride. If there is division in your circles, ask God how you can be a peacemaker. Unity is worth the effort. It is good, and it is pleasant.
question: Where could you help build unity today instead of division?
prayer: Lord, how good and how pleasant it is when Your people dwell together in unity. Make me a peacemaker today, and help me join others rather than divide them. Amen.

text: And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
reflection: Joshua was old, and his years of leading Israel were nearly over. He gathered the people and reminded them of everything God had done. Then he put a choice before them: "choose you this day whom ye will serve." Some still clung to the idols of their ancestors or of the land around them. Joshua would not force anyone's heart, but he made his own position clear: "but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD." This is a decision every household must make. Not only once, but again and again. What will be at the center of our home? What will shape our priorities, conversations, and use of time? The idols today may look different, such as success, entertainment, comfort, or approval. But the choice is the same. Joshua's declaration was public and firm. He set the direction for his family. Today, make that choice for yourself and your home. Decide again whom you will serve.
question: What do you want to be at the center of your home, and what choice today would show it?
prayer: Lord, as for me and my house, we will serve You. Help me choose You again today, and let my home be a place where You are honoured. Amen.

text: She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness.
reflection: Proverbs 31 paints a portrait of a capable, godly woman. She works hard, manages her household wisely, cares for the poor, and is respected in her community. Among all her qualities, this one stands out: "She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness." Her words are governed by kindness. It is not an occasional habit but a law, a settled rule of her speech. She speaks with wisdom, but never harshly. Her words build up rather than tear down. This is a beautiful goal for anyone. Our homes are shaped by the words spoken in them. Kind words create safety and warmth. Harsh words create fear and distance. Imagine making kindness the law of your tongue, so that before you speak, you ask whether your words are both wise and kind. Today, pay attention to how you speak to the people you live and work with. Let kindness rule your tongue.
question: How could kindness govern the way you speak at home today?
prayer: Lord, let the law of kindness be on my tongue. Fill my words with wisdom and gentleness, and let them make my home a warmer place today. Amen.

text: And David said unto him, Fear not: for I will surely shew thee kindness for Jonathan thy father's sake, and will restore thee all the land of Saul thy father; and thou shalt eat bread at my table continually.
reflection: Years after Jonathan died, King David asked a remarkable question: was anyone left from Saul's family to whom he could show kindness for Jonathan's sake? A servant told him about Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, who was lame in both feet and living in obscurity. In those days, a new king often eliminated the previous king's family. Mephibosheth must have been terrified when he was summoned. But David said, "Fear not: for I will surely shew thee kindness for Jonathan thy father's sake." David restored his family land and gave him a permanent place at the royal table. Mephibosheth could not repay this. He had done nothing to earn it. It was pure kindness, flowing from love for his friend. This story paints a picture of God's grace toward us. We come to Him with nothing to offer, and He welcomes us to His table. Today, look for a way to show undeserved kindness to someone, perhaps for the sake of someone you love.
question: Who could you show undeserved kindness to today, as God has shown it to you?
prayer: Lord, You sought me out and gave me a place at Your table when I deserved nothing. Help me show that same kindness to someone else today. Amen.

text: Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another, even as also ye do.
reflection: Paul wrote to the believers in Thessalonica, who were facing persecution and grieving loved ones who had died. After teaching them about the hope of Christ's return, he gave them a job to do: "Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another, even as also ye do." To comfort means to encourage and strengthen. To edify means to build up, like constructing a house brick by brick. Paul noticed they were already doing this, and he urged them to keep going. Encouragement is not a small thing. In a discouraging world, a kind word can give someone the strength to keep going. A note, a message, or a sincere compliment can lift a heavy heart. We often think of encouraging words but never say them. Today, do not let that happen. Think of someone who could use encouragement and tell them what you appreciate about them, or how you have seen God at work in their life. Build them up.
question: What encouraging words have you been thinking about someone that you could say out loud today?
prayer: Lord, help me comfort and build up the people around me. Let me speak the encouraging words I have been holding back, and strengthen someone through them. Amen.

text: And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works…
reflection: The word provoke usually has a negative meaning. We provoke someone to anger. But the writer of Hebrews uses it in a positive way: "And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works." To consider means to think carefully about, to pay attention. We are to study one another, getting to know each other well enough to know how to stir each other toward love and good deeds. What encourages one person may not encourage another. Some need a challenge. Others need a reminder of their gifts. Others need an example to follow. This verse also assumes that we are close enough to one another to do this. It is hard to stir someone toward good works from a distance. That is why the next verse urges believers not to neglect meeting together. Today, think about one person you know well. How could you inspire them toward love and good works? Then do it.
question: Who is one person you could stir up toward love and good works today?
prayer: Lord, help me consider the people around me with care. Show me how to stir someone toward love and good works, and keep us close to one another. Amen.

text: Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
reflection: Hospitality was essential in the ancient world. Travellers depended on the kindness of strangers for food and shelter. The writer of Hebrews reminds believers, "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." He was likely thinking of Abraham, who welcomed three visitors and later learned they were messengers from God. The point is not that every stranger is an angel. It is that kindness to strangers matters to God, and we never know how He might use it. Showing hospitality can feel risky or inconvenient today. Our lives are busy, and our homes may feel too small or too messy. But hospitality is more than hosting dinner parties. It is a welcoming spirit. It might mean greeting a newcomer, helping someone who is lost, or sitting with someone who is alone. The word forgetful is a gentle warning. It is easy to overlook strangers. Today, notice them. Offer a welcome.
question: Who is new or unfamiliar around you that you could welcome today?
prayer: Lord, help me not to forget kindness to strangers. Open my eyes to someone new around me, and let me welcome them as You have welcomed me. Amen.

text: Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God; and every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God.
reflection: Today is a day that comes only once every four years, a little extra time tucked into the calendar. What better way to spend it than with these words from John: "Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God; and every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God." John was an old man when he wrote this letter, and love was his constant theme. He had leaned on Jesus at the table and stood near the cross. He knew love was not merely a feeling or a good idea. Love is of God. It flows from His very nature. When we truly love, we show that we know Him and belong to Him. This month we have reflected on friendship, kindness, and family. All of it springs from this source. We love because God first loved us. Use this extra day well. Do something loving that you would not otherwise have done. Let it be a small gift back to the God who is love.
question: What loving thing could you do with this extra day that you would not otherwise have done?
prayer: Lord, love is of You, and everyone who loves is born of You and knows You. Thank You for this extra day. Let me spend some of it loving someone well. Amen.
